content: Juglans nigra, commonly referred to as black walnut or American walnut, is a tree species indigenous to eastern North America. It predominantly grows along riverbanks, ranging from southern Ontario, Canada, westward to southeastern South Dakota, southward to Georgia and northern Florida, and southwest to central Texas. This species is a large deciduous tree, capable of reaching heights of 30 to 40 meters (100 to 130 feet). When growing in forested areas with competition, it develops a tall, straight trunk (bole), whereas in open areas, it forms a shorter trunk with a broad crown. The bark is gray-black in color and deeply furrowed. The twigs of the tree contain pith with air spaces. The leaves of the black walnut are alternate, measuring 30 to 60 cm in length, and are odd-pinnate with 15 to 23 leaflets. The largest leaflets are located in the center, measuring 7 to 10 cm in length and 2 to 3 cm in width. Male flowers are borne in drooping catkins that are 8 to 10 cm long, while female flowers are terminal and occur in clusters of two to five. These flowers mature in the autumn into fruits with a brownish-green, semi-fleshy husk and a brown, corrugated nut. The entire fruit, including the husk, falls in October. The seed inside is relatively small and encased in a very hard shell. The black walnut was introduced to Europe in 1629, where it is cultivated as a forest tree for its high-quality wood. It is more frost-resistant than the Persian walnut but thrives best in warmer regions of Europe with fertile, lowland soils that have high water availability. This species requires ample sunlight for optimal growth. The wood of the black walnut is highly valued for making furniture and rifle stocks, while oil is extracted from its seeds. The black walnut produces a chemical compound called juglone, which is toxic or allelopathic to many other plants. Juglone disrupts the healthy development of nearby plants, often causing wilting and yellowing of their foliage. This has led to the misconception that no plants can grow beneath a black walnut tree. However, many plant species are tolerant of juglone. Interestingly, fescue grass exhibits allelopathic effects against the black walnut itself. Use as Food Extracting the kernel from the fruit of the black walnut is a challenging process. The nut is encased in a thick husk that exudes a dark, staining, and strong-smelling juice. Initially yellow-brown, the juice quickly turns a deep black-green upon exposure to air. The shell often intrudes into the kernel, making it difficult to obtain whole kernels. The husk is best removed when it is still green, as this improves the flavor of the nuts. A common method for husk removal involves rolling the nut underfoot on a hard surface, such as a driveway. Commercial huskers use a car tire rotating against a metal mesh. Another method involves drilling a nut-sized hole (1 to 2 inches in diameter) into a thick plywood board and hammering the nut through, leaving the husk behind. To prevent the husk juice from splattering, a board or canvas scrap can be used to cover the nut during hammering. The husks of black walnuts are notorious for leaving long-lasting stains on hands and clothing. Before consumption or storage, the nuts should be cured in a dry place for at least two weeks. To facilitate cracking, the unshelled nuts can be soaked in hot water for 24 hours to soften the shells, although this step is unnecessary with a proper nutcracker. Despite the prized flavor of black walnuts, the difficulty in preparing them may explain the greater popularity and availability of Persian walnuts. Wood The wood of the black walnut is highly esteemed for its dark-colored true heartwood. It is heavy and strong, yet it can be easily split and worked. Historically, walnut wood has been used for crafting gunstocks, furniture, flooring, paddles, coffins, and various other woodworking products. Due to its high value, forestry officials are often tasked with tracking down walnut poachers. In one notable case in 2004, DNA testing was employed to solve a poaching incident involving a 55-foot (16-meter) black walnut tree valued at an estimated $2,500.
